title: The butcher who taught a scholar
hookLine: A proud scholar is sent to a butcher to learn dharma, and finds a duty for everyone.
carry: your own dharma differs; the dharma for all doesn't
tomorrow: a book well-known for one thing has a chapter on another. which?

lines: A PROUD SCHOLAR, A DEAD CRANE.
GO LEARN DHARMA FROM A BUTCHER.
cards: The Mahabharata tells of Kaushika, a young brahmin who has studied the Vedas and grown proud of his power. A crane soils him from a branch above, and with one angry look he burns it dead.
Then he goes begging for food at a house, and the woman there makes him wait while she cares for her husband. When she finally comes out, he's furious. She answers calmly: I'm not a crane.
You know the Vedas, but not dharma. Go to Mithila, and learn it from the vyadha there, a man who sells meat in the market. So the scholar goes to a butcher's stall to be taught.

teach.b: The butcher, the dharma-vyadha, welcomes him, and his teaching fills chapters of the Mahabharata. He does the work his family has always done, he says, and does it honestly. He serves his aged parents.
He speaks the truth and gives what he can. Then he sends Kaushika home to care for the parents he left behind. Hindu teaching names both halves of that.

Svadharma is your own duty, by your role and stage of life, and the Arthashastra's chapter on the Vedas spends most of its length there: the student's duties, the householder's, the ruler's, and duties tied to birth.
Then, in one line, it names duties common to all: not harming, truthfulness, purity, freedom from spite, freedom from cruelty, and forgiveness.
Hindu teachers call this sadharana dharma, the dharma for everyone. Read beside this chapter, the story puts its weight on that floor.

teach.h: THE SCHOLAR FAILED IT; THE BUTCHER KEPT IT.
teach.b: The scholar held the honored station and failed the shared list: cruel to a bird, angry at a woman for making him wait.
The butcher, in a trade many looked down on, kept it. Some readers through the centuries leaned on the stations, especially where station meant rank by birth, the ranking Ambedkar refused.
Many teachers read this story as the tradition's own answer to that pride.

how: Hindu teachers distinguish svadharma, the duties of one's own station and stage of life, from sadharana dharma, duties common to everyone; the Mahabharata's story of the dharma-vyadha is often told to make the point.

o: an old ruling book's start: one single rule for every person
an old ruling book's start: a ruler's own duties come first
an old ruling book's start: duties by role, and a list for all

games.q: one chapter, two readings — tap the pairs.
p: your own duty, by role and stage
no harm, truth, no cruelty, forgiveness
knew the Vedas, burned a crane

s: the Arthashastra only has duties that depend on your station
one line names duties common to all: not harming, truthfulness, purity, no spite, no cruelty, forgiveness.
the butcher sent the scholar home to care for his own aged parents
Kaushika had left them to study; serving them was the duty he'd skipped.
in the Mahabharata, the butcher goes to the proud scholar to learn dharma
it's the other way round: the scholar is sent to the butcher, who teaches him and sends him home to his parents.

games.q: at a new job, a senior manager says, 'my role is different, so the usual rules on honesty bend for me.' by this chapter of the Arthashastra, what's the answer?
o: true: higher roles carry different duties, honesty included.
no: truthfulness is on the list for everyone, whatever the role.
it depends on how senior the manager is.
games.why: roles bring their own duties, but the chapter's shared list, not harming, truthfulness, no cruelty and the rest, is for everyone.

practice: Close your eyes if that's comfortable. On each slow breath, bring to mind one role you hold, child, friend, student, worker, and one duty that comes with it.
For the last few breaths, let the roles fall away, and rest on what you'd owe anyone at all: the truth, and no cruelty.
If you see a parent or elder today, many Hindu families greet them by touching their feet; you might, or simply call them.

wordCard.voice: The Arthashastra's opening: each person's own duty, and under every station a short list for all, from not harming to forgiveness.

orig.note: Sanskrit svadharma, one's own duty: the duties of a person's station and stage of life.

carryVoice: Keep this: your own dharma differs; the dharma for all doesn't. A butcher taught a scholar that. That's the end of this run.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Aranyaka (Vana) Parva (Kaushika, the crane and the faithful wife; the dharma-vyadha of Mithila teaches him and sends him home to his parents)
Arthashastra 1.3 (the duties of each varna and ashrama; duties common to all: ahimsa, satya, shaucha, anasuya, anrishamsya, kshama)
